strings.name: Nana Akufo-Addo
strings.role: Former president of Ghana and lawyer
strings.summary: Nana Akufo-Addo is a Ghanaian lawyer and New Patriotic Party politician who served as an MP, attorney-general and justice minister, and foreign minister before becoming president from 2017 to 2025. His government introduced Free Senior High School education and One District One Factory, while he chaired the ECOWAS Authority of Heads of State and Government from 2020 to 2022. His second presidential term faced a severe fiscal and debt crisis and entry into an IMF-supported programme. He continues public engagement after leaving office.
strings.coverageNote: Sources checked through November 18, 2026, with recent activity confirmed through November 17. The account distinguishes father and son, elections and inaugurations, the rotating ECOWAS Authority chair and Commission president, programme launches and results, and approved financing from actual disbursements.
strings.influence.rationale: He led ECOWAS and participated in responses to regional coup crises, while advancing education and industrial policies in Ghana, giving him influence in West Africa.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and economics education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in Accra on March 29, 1944. His father, Edward Akufo-Addo, served as Ghana's ceremonial president. He entered the University of Ghana to study economics in 1964 and earned a bachelor's degree in 1967. The alumni webpage explicitly reproduces Wikipedia and is not equivalent to an original academic record; admission to the bar is also not a separately verified university law degree.
strings.facts.f2.label: Legal practice and party career
strings.facts.f2.value: Called to the English bar in 1971 and the Ghanaian bar in 1975, he worked at Coudert Brothers in Paris and a law practice in Accra before co-founding Akufo-Addo, Prempeh & Co. in 1979. He joined the New Patriotic Party in 1992 and was elected three times as MP for Abuakwa South. He lost the 2008 and 2012 presidential contests before winning in 2016.
strings.highlights.h1.title: One District One Factory industrial policy
strings.highlights.h1.text: The Finance Ministry's 2018 Citizens’ Budget records his launch of One District One Factory on August 25, 2017, and government technical, financial and commercial assessments of project proposals. Selected proposals, planned factories and expected jobs represent different stages. The programme's name does not prove that every district received a completed, continuously operating factory.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Maintains dialogue with his successor
strings.highlights.h2.text: On November 17, 2026, he received President John Dramani Mahama at his Nima residence in Accra. MyJoyOnline reported discussions of domestic and international matters, with Mahama accompanied by staff. No specific agreement was disclosed, so the meeting does not establish a new appointment or policy decision.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Hands the presidency to Mahama
strings.timeline.t1.text: After completing two presidential terms, he left office as Mahama, winner of the December 2024 election, was sworn in. Mahama was also the predecessor he had replaced in 2017 and was returning to power. Akufo-Addo is no longer the incumbent president.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Government enters an IMF-supported programme
strings.timeline.t2.text: The IMF Executive Board approved an approximately US$3 billion Extended Credit Facility arrangement, initially lasting 36 months, with about US$600 million available for immediate disbursement to support macroeconomic stability and debt restructuring. The IMF described external shocks aggravating existing fiscal and debt weaknesses. The total was not paid out that day, and approval did not mean the crisis was resolved.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Begins his second presidential term
strings.timeline.t3.text: Following re-election on December 7, 2020, he was sworn in on January 7, 2021, with Mahamudu Bawumia continuing as vice-president. Election and inauguration took place on different dates, and this was his final presidential term.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Becomes rotating ECOWAS Authority chair
strings.timeline.t4.text: At the 57th summit in Niamey, he succeeded Niger's Mahamadou Issoufou as chair of the ECOWAS Authority of Heads of State and Government. He served until Embaló took over on July 3, 2022, amid regional coup and security crises. This was not the ECOWAS Commission presidency, nor does the tenure establish that all crises were resolved.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Introduces Free Senior High School education
strings.timeline.t5.text: From the September 2017 school year, the government covered relevant fees for eligible first-year public senior-high-school students, extending coverage to later cohorts over time. Education authorities implemented the policy while managing classroom, accommodation and quality pressures. The aim of expanding access does not establish that all educational inequalities disappeared.
strings.timeline.t6.title: First takes office as president of Ghana
strings.timeline.t6.text: After winning the December 7, 2016 presidential election for the New Patriotic Party, he succeeded Mahama and took the oath on January 7, 2017. He had lost the 2008 runoff to Mills and the 2012 election to Mahama. The legal challenge to the 2012 result did not overturn Mahama's victory, and Akufo-Addo subsequently accepted the court's decision.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Moves to the foreign ministry
strings.timeline.t7.text: Under President John Kufuor, he moved from the justice portfolio to foreign affairs, serving until 2007 and participating in West African multilateral affairs and regional diplomacy. He then left government to seek his party's presidential nomination. Ministerial service, party nomination and becoming president were separate stages.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Becomes attorney-general and justice minister
strings.timeline.t8.text: He served as attorney-general and minister of justice in Kufuor's government until 2003, helping advance repeal of criminal-libel provisions and judicial reform. His legal practice and government legal work are distinct from his later foreign-minister and presidential duties; these posts did not make him a judge or chief justice.
